strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: user-level privacy for federated speech recognition. Speaker-partitioned datasets and LibriSpeech-to-Common-Voice adaptation provide a useful benchmark with substantial client heterogeneity and domain shift.

The non-private experiments are extensive, covering initialization, cohort size, optimizers, normalization, data heterogeneity, augmentation, and three languages. Several pretrained configurations approach centralized accuracy within 2,000 aggregation rounds, and transferring hyperparameters across languages is encouraging.

Revisiting per-layer clipping yields a useful empirical insight. At the same clipping bound and injected noise, Table 2 improves English test WER from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based clipping while preserving the overall update-norm bound.

The appendix provides substantial training details, diagnostic experiments, and compute costs. The authors explicitly disclose the population extrapolation and acknowledge existing work on per-layer clipping. Public research datasets support accessibility, with no evident serious ethical concern.
weaknesses: The headline privacy–utility results are not demonstrated experimentally at useful privacy levels. The relevant WERs are measured with 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024, where the reported epsilon values are approximately 10^7–10^8. Obtaining epsilon 4.5 or 7.2 requires extrapolating to roughly 7 million or 70 million users and cohorts of 204,800 while assuming comparable training utility. Although clearly disclosed, this assumption lacks empirical scaling validation or theoretical support. This gap in the central contribution is the main reason for rejection.

The privacy accounting needs to match the implemented mechanism. Algorithm 1 specifies Bernoulli sampling but states that experiments fix the cohort size, while Theorem 1 invokes the sampled-Gaussian accountant with sensitivity C/(qN). The Bernoulli pseudocode also divides by the realized cohort size. These sampling and normalization choices require a matching analysis under the stated add/remove-user adjacency; the reported guarantees are not fully justified as written.

The claim of nearly optimal federated training, including training without a seed, is too broad. In Table 4, training Common Voice English from scratch reaches 25.7% test WER at the largest tested cohort, compared with 18.2% centrally—a 7.5 percentage-point gap. The strong conclusions should distinguish successful pretrained configurations from the substantially weaker from-scratch results.

The explanation underlying the clipping insight remains incomplete. The main text emphasizes attention parameters being overwhelmed by noise, whereas Appendix D.5 and Figures 16–17 identify MLP parameters as the most sensitive. Moreover, Table 17 shows only 0.1–0.2 percentage-point improvements over global clipping for German and French. These findings need reconciliation to establish when the benefit should generalize.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix: code is only promised, exact random user-partition artifacts are not supplied, and WER results lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates. These omissions particularly affect the proposed benchmark's reuse and confidence in marginal improvements.
